overview.title: Preparing Reuters inputs and one-hot labels; why 46 classes change the model
overview.section: 4.2 Classifying newswires: A multiclass classification example
overview.main_topic: Multi-hot encoding of inputs, one-hot (categorical) encoding of the 46-class labels by hand and with to_categorical, and the information-bottleneck argument for larger intermediate layers
overview.central_idea: Inputs are vectorised exactly as for IMDb. Labels can stay integers or be one-hot encoded: an all-zero vector of length 46 with a 1 at the label index. Because the output space now has 46 dimensions instead of 2, small intermediate Dense layers risk discarding information that later layers can never recover.
overview.importance: One-hot encoding is the standard target format for categorical crossentropy. The bottleneck argument is the first architectural principle the book gives for choosing layer width, and it is tested experimentally on p.149.
learning_objectives: Apply multi_hot_encode to produce 10,000-dimensional input vectors for Reuters
Define one-hot (categorical) encoding and implement it with NumPy
Use keras.utils.to_categorical as the built-in equivalent
Name the two label options (integers vs. one-hot) and the loss each goes with
Explain why a Dense stack cannot recover information dropped by an earlier, narrower layer

summary:
**4.2.2 Preparing the data.** The inputs are vectorised "with the exact same code as in the previous example". **Listing 4.13** calls `multi_hot_encode(train_data, num_classes=10000)` and the same for `test_data`, giving `x_train` with shape (8982, 10000) and `x_test` with shape (2246, 10000) of 0/1 values.

For the **labels** there are two options: leave them **as integers**, or use **one-hot encoding**, also called **categorical encoding**, a widely used format for categorical data. Here it means embedding each label as **an all-zero vector with a 1 at the label index**. **Listing 4.14** defines `one_hot_encode(labels, num_classes=46)`. It allocates `np.zeros((len(labels), num_classes))`, sets `results[i, label] = 1.0` for each sample, and returns the matrix. It is applied to `train_labels` and `test_labels` to get `y_train` (8982, 46) and `y_test` (2246, 46). Keras has a built-in way to do the same: `keras.utils.to_categorical`.

**4.2.3 Building your model.** The problem looks like the movie-review problem, since both classify short snippets of text, but there is a new constraint: the number of output classes has gone **from 2 to 46**, so the output space has many more dimensions. In a stack of `Dense` layers, **each layer can only access information present in the output of the previous layer**. If one layer drops information relevant to the classification, later layers cannot recover it (the sentence finishes on p.143, which goes on to call each layer a potential **information bottleneck** and to choose 64-unit layers instead of 16).

paragraphs.what_it_says: There are two ways to vectorise the labels: keep them as integers, or one-hot encode them. One-hot (categorical) encoding is widely used for categorical data. Here it means representing each label as an all-zero vector with a 1 at the label index.

paragraphs.what_it_says: In a Dense stack each layer only sees the previous layer's output. If a layer drops information relevant to classification, that information can never be... (continued on p.143: '...recovered by later layers').
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is a data-processing argument. Each layer is a function of the previous layer's output only, so later layers can rearrange information but cannot recreate what was lost. A 16-dimensional layer computes relu(W x + b) with W of shape 10000 x 16; it can preserve at most 16 directions of variation of the input. If separating 46 topics requires more than that, the information is gone.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets up the 'information bottleneck' principle on p.143 and the 4-unit bottleneck experiment on p.149, which loses about 8 points of validation accuracy.
paragraphs.technical_idea: In a sequential stack, the information a layer can pass on is limited by the width of the narrowest earlier layer.

terminology.meaning: A layer too narrow to carry all the task-relevant information forward (term introduced on p.143).

concepts.name: One-hot (categorical) encoding
concepts.definition: Representing a categorical label as an all-zero vector with a single 1 at the position of the label index.
concepts.intuition: A row of 46 light switches with exactly one turned on.
concepts.technical: For label y among K classes, the target is e_y in {0,1}^K, with entry j equal to 1 if j = y and 0 otherwise. Stacked over N samples, this gives an (N, K) matrix. It is the target format expected by categorical_crossentropy and has the same shape as a K-way softmax output.
concepts.significance: It turns category ids into probability-distribution-shaped targets and avoids imposing a false order on the categories.
concepts.misconception: One-hot is not required for multiclass training; integer labels with sparse_categorical_crossentropy are equivalent (p.148).

concepts.name: Multi-hot encoding of the inputs
concepts.definition: Each newswire becomes a 10,000-dimensional vector with 1s at the indices of the words it contains.
concepts.intuition: A checklist of the vocabulary with a tick next to every word that appears.
concepts.technical: x[i, w] = 1 if word w appears in sample i. This gives x_train with shape (8982, 10000) and x_test with shape (2246, 10000). It discards word order and counts.
concepts.significance: It gives fixed-size vector inputs for a Dense network, using the same code as IMDb.
concepts.example: train_data[10] has 31 tokens, some repeated, so its row has at most 31 ones (fewer, because of the repeats).
concepts.misconception: Multi-hot (many 1s, for the input) and one-hot (exactly one 1, for the label) are different encodings.

concepts.name: Information bottleneck in a Dense stack
concepts.definition: Because each layer only sees the previous layer's output, information dropped by one layer cannot be recovered by later layers. Too-narrow layers become bottlenecks.
concepts.intuition: A bucket brigade: if one person uses a small cup, everyone after them can carry only that much water, however big their own buckets are.
concepts.technical: The layer h2 = f(h1) depends only on h1. A width-d layer has image dimension at most d, so if separating 46 classes needs more than d dimensions, accuracy is permanently limited.
concepts.significance: It gives a rule for width: intermediate layers should not be much narrower than the number of output classes.
concepts.example: p.149: replacing the 64-unit layers with 4-unit ones drops peak validation accuracy to about 71%.
concepts.misconception: Making the last layer bigger does not fix a narrow earlier layer; information lost upstream is lost for good.

code.title: Encoding the labels
code.original_code:
def one_hot_encode(labels, num_classes=46):
    results = np.zeros((len(labels), num_classes))
    for i, label in enumerate(labels):
        results[i, label] = 1.0
    return results

y_train = one_hot_encode(train_labels)
y_test = one_hot_encode(test_labels)
code.what_it_does: Implements one-hot encoding by hand for the 46 topic labels and applies it to the training and test labels ('Vectorized training labels', 'Vectorized test labels').

line_explanations.explanation: Function taking an array of integer labels; 46 classes by default.
Allocates an all-zero float matrix of shape (number of samples, 46).
For sample i with label label, put a 1.0 in column label.
y_train has shape (8982, 46) and y_test shape (2246, 46).

code.inputs_outputs: Input: int arrays with values 0-45. Output: float64 arrays of shape (N, 46) with exactly one 1.0 per row.
code.algorithm: Indicator encoding with a Python loop. Beyond the book, it could be vectorised as results[np.arange(N), labels] = 1.
code.theory_link: Produces the 'true distribution' that categorical_crossentropy compares with the softmax output (p.143).

parameters.role: Can be passed explicitly (e.g. 46) to avoid relying on the largest label present.

deeper.body:
| array | shape | content |
|---|---|---|
| `x_train` | (8982, 10000) | multi-hot words |
| `x_test` | (2246, 10000) | multi-hot words |
| `y_train` | (8982, 46) | one-hot topics |

`x_train` has about 90 million entries, about 718 MB as float64 (or 359 MB as float32). Most are 0, since each newswire uses only a few dozen to a few hundred distinct words. (Sizes computed here; not in the book.)

deeper.title: Why the narrowest layer limits everything after it
deeper.body:
1. A Dense layer with $d$ units maps its input to $\mathbb{R}^d$.
2. Everything later in the stack depends on the input **only through** those $d$ numbers.
3. If two newswires on different topics produce the same (or nearly the same) $d$-vector, no later layer can tell them apart.
4. With 46 topics to separate, a $d=16$ representation may merge some topics that a $d=64$ representation would keep apart.

That is why the book raises the width to 64 on p.143 and shows the cost of $d=4$ on p.149. (Expanded explanation; the core argument is the book's.)

deeper.title: Two kinds of hot
deeper.body: A **multi-hot** input is like a shopping receipt that ticks every product bought: many ticks are possible. A **one-hot** label is like the single department a store files the receipt under: exactly one tick. The model reads the receipt and has to guess the department.

takeaways: Reuters inputs are vectorised with the IMDb code: multi_hot_encode(..., num_classes=10000).
Labels can stay integers or be one-hot (categorical) encoded: an all-zero vector of length 46 with a 1 at the label index.
keras.utils.to_categorical does the same thing as the hand-written one_hot_encode.
Going from 2 to 46 output classes makes the output space much larger, and the hidden layers must carry enough information.
In a Dense stack, information dropped by one layer cannot be recovered by later layers.

questions.question: What is the shape of y_train after listing 4.14?
questions.explanation: One row per training sample and one column per topic. (8982,) is the raw integer labels; (8982, 10000) is x_train; the transposed shape is wrong.

questions.question: Define one-hot encoding of a label as the book does.
questions.answer: Embedding each label as an all-zero vector with a 1 in the place of the label index; also called categorical encoding.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly on the page. For Reuters the vectors have length 46.

questions.question: Write the one-hot vector for label 0 and for label 45 with 46 classes. What do all one-hot vectors sum to?
questions.answer: Label 0 gives [1, 0, ..., 0]; label 45 gives [0, ..., 0, 1] (46 entries each). Every one-hot vector sums to 1.
questions.explanation: Exactly one entry is 1, so each one-hot vector is a valid probability distribution with all its mass on the true class.

questions.question: What are the two options the page gives for vectorising the labels?
options: Leaving them as integers or one-hot encoding them
One-hot encoding or embedding them with an Embedding layer
Scaling them to [0, 1] or one-hot encoding them
questions.answer: Leaving them as integers or one-hot encoding them
questions.explanation: The page says 'you can leave the labels untouched as integers, or you can use one-hot encoding'. Multi-hot is for inputs; embeddings and scaling are not discussed for labels.

questions.question: Explain in your own words why information dropped by one Dense layer can never be recovered by later layers.
questions.answer: Each layer computes its output only from the previous layer's output. Later layers have no access to the original input, so if two inputs become indistinguishable after a narrow layer, nothing downstream can separate them again.
questions.explanation: This is the argument started on this page and finished on p.143; p.149 demonstrates it experimentally.

questions.question: In listing 4.13 the argument is num_classes=10000, and in listing 4.14 it is num_classes=46. What does 'classes' mean in each case?
questions.answer: In 4.13 the 'classes' are vocabulary indices (the 10,000 words kept), so the input vector length. In 4.14 they are the 46 newswire topics, so the label vector length.
questions.explanation: The same keyword name is used for two different things, a common source of confusion.

questions.question: Could you rewrite one_hot_encode without a Python loop, and check that it gives the same result as to_categorical?
questions.answer: Yes: results = np.zeros((N, 46)); results[np.arange(N), labels] = 1.0; then compare with np.allclose(results, to_categorical(labels)).
questions.explanation: If this is unclear, review NumPy fancy indexing; the result must have exactly one 1 per row at the label position.
